newsitem.title: MEXICO: Rebel groups in Mexico said multiplying.
newsitem.headline: Rebel groups in Mexico said multiplying.
newsitem.dateline: SAN CRISTOBAL DE LAS CASAS, Mexico 1996-11-14

text.p: Zapatista Rebel leader Subcommander Marcos said on Thursday that three or four new guerrilla bands have sprung up in Mexico in addition to his group and the newer Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR).

"There are three or four armed groups that the government does not want to recognise in (the states of) Hidalgo, Oaxaca, Veracruz and Puebla," Marcos told a news conference in this colonial city in the southern state of Chiapas.
The Zapatistas first took up arms in Chiapas 1994 and were followed this year by the EPR in the southern state of Oaxaca.

The charismatic Marcos said hardliners within the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) were dividing Mexico further between the rich and the poor, forcing some to take up arms in order to have their demands heard.

"This radicalization ... and appearance of new guerrilla groups is caused by the desperation of some sectors and the voices in the government that ask for a hard line," the masked, pipe-smoking rebel leader said.
"In Mexico there is the feeling that only if you take up arms is anyone going to listen to you," Marcos said.

Some 150 people died during the Zapatista rebellion in early 1994, but the rebels and government have been in peace talks ever since. The EPR has launched sporadic attacks on military targets in several states since its appearance for the first time in June.

Marcos reiterated his group's demand that peace talks with the government be moved out of the southern state of Chiapas, charging that the state government has been trying to sabotage the peace process by cracking down on peasant supporters of the mostly Indian movement.
"The conditions don't exist in Chiapas. Either they are changed to another place or we will definitely withdraw from the negotiations," Marcos said.

The Zapatistas pulled out of peace talks in September, charging that government negotiators were inflexible and racist. The rebels came to this city from their jungle hideouts this week to negotiate a return to talks through a legislative commission.
